rationale: PGS001135 is better supported on PRS-comparable evidence: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC (0.539) and PGS-only R² (0.00291), which are interpretable and below the arthritis heritability ceiling, and it uses only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array). It also has broader evaluation ancestry coverage (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS), supporting transportability. In contrast, PGS004477 has no AUC/R² reported at all (only an OR=1.20, which suggests weak PRS signal), unknown covariates, and EUR-only evaluation, so its standalone PRS performance and comparability are much less evidenced despite its genome-wide variant count.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_efo=atopic eczema; phenotyping_reported=incident atopic dermatitis) and have identical covariates and validation size (n=337,910 EUR), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either, so metrics don’t differentiate cleanly. Structurally, PGS002755 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with ~1.09M variants, which is generally better suited to a polygenic trait like atopic eczema than PGS004587’s 23 genome-wide significant SNP score. The observed HR separation is also slightly stronger for PGS002755 (HR 1.249 vs 1.153). PGS004587 lists multiple training cohorts, but without PRS-comparable performance this is weaker evidence than the large structural/method advantage of PGS002755.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context: same reported/phenotyped trait (M13 Other arthritis), same EFO (arthritis), same training cohort (UKB), identical training/validation sizes and EUR-only DEV/EVAL, and both lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2 with covariates listed as Unknown. With metrics otherwise missing, the main differentiator is the reported per-SD effect size: PGS004547 shows a higher OR (1.262198) than PGS004477 (1.1956), indicating stronger PRS signal in the available evidence. Method_name also favors PGS004547 structurally (metaPRS-style aggregation) over the single-score LDpred2 sibling when all else is equal.

Both candidates come from the same Nat Genet study, use the same method (PRS-CS), have identical evaluation context (EUR-only; incident aortic stenosis; same basic covariates; same validation sample size n=244,450), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the decision rests on endpoint/label alignment and effect-size strength. PGS005254 is the direct aortic stenosis score (trait_reported/trait_efo both aortic stenosis) and shows a stronger HR per SD (1.64, 95% CI 1.50–1.78) than PGS005255 (HR 1.53, 1.40–1.66), with also a larger training sample (205,483 vs 98,645). PGS005255’s trait_reported is a measurement (mean pressure gradient) with a broader/mixed trait_efo mapping, making it slightly less faithful to the target trait despite the same incident AS evaluation.

PGS001135 is better supported on PRS-comparable evidence: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC (0.539) and PGS-only R² (0.00291), allowing a clean comparison and a heritability-ceiling sanity check, and it uses only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array). It also has broader evaluation ancestry coverage (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS), which is supportive for transportability. In contrast, PGS004547 has no PRS-comparable performance metrics (AUC/R² all null) and only a modest OR (1.26) with unknown covariates, making its predictive value and comparability harder to judge despite being more genome-wide and from a disease/risk-factor integration framing.

Both candidates align well to the target (trait_efo = alcoholic liver cirrhosis; phenotyping_reported is a direct alcoholic/alcohol-associated cirrhosis endpoint). However, PGS004913 is a disease-focused score explicitly developed for alcohol-associated cirrhosis among heavy drinkers, and it provides PRS-relevant effect evidence (OR top vs bottom deciles = 4.4) plus an R²=0.029 (though not explicitly labeled PGS-only, it is at least a PRS-attributable metric and is plausible under the heritability ceiling). In contrast, PGS000704 comes from a broad UKB biomarker genetics framework context and only reports a full-model C-index (0.711) plus a modest HR=1.18, with no PRS-only AUC/R²; the C-index is not PRS-comparable and likely covariate-driven. Given stronger endpoint-focused study context and stronger PRS effect signal, PGS004913 is better supported on the visible fields.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target trait (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported = abdominal aortic aneurysm; same method PRS-CS; same variant count; same GWAS/EVAL ancestry context). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model metrics are only weakly informative. Given that, PGS003973 is better-supported because it at least discloses basic covariates (Age, Age^2, Sex), making its reported C-index=0.882 interpretable as a demographic-adjusted model, whereas PGS003972 has covariates listed as Unknown and a lower reported AUROC=0.69. Validation sample sizes are similar (7,517 vs 6,940) and training cohorts differ only marginally, so they don’t outweigh the clearer covariate reporting and stronger (albeit full-model) discrimination in PGS003973.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo are aortic stenosis; phenotyping is incident aortic stenosis) and are EUR-only in development/evaluation, and neither reports PRS-comparable PGS-only AUC/R2 (so PGS005252’s full-model C-index=0.87 is not usable as a PRS metric, especially given its heavy clinical covariate set). With PRS-only metrics absent for both, the best comparable evidence is the per-SD effect size and covariate cleanliness: PGS005254 reports HR=1.64 (95% CI 1.50–1.78) with only basic demographic/PC covariates, whereas PGS005252 reports a higher HR=1.92 but alongside extensive comorbidity/risk-factor covariates (T2D, HTN, CAD, hyperlipidemia, BMI, smoking, renal failure), making its reported performance signals more confounded and less comparable to standalone PRS use. Given similar endpoint fidelity, PGS005254 is better-supported as a cleaner PRS evaluation despite the slightly smaller HR.

Both candidates match the target trait well (trait_reported/trait_efo are AAA). However, PGS003972 is structurally much stronger for a complex disease PRS: it uses genome-wide shrinkage (PRS-CS) with ~1.1M variants and is derived from a large multi-cohort GWAS meta-analysis context, whereas PGS000753 is a very sparse P+T score with only 29 variants. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use comparable discrimination metrics; in that setting, domain guidance favors method/variant-count signals. PGS000753 does report an OR per SD of 1.37 (moderate), but it is still a sparse model and its endpoint is explicitly prevalent AAA, while PGS003972 uses a generic AAA phenotype and avoids explicit covariate packaging (covariates unknown, but no evidence of heavy clinical leakage). Overall, PGS003972 has better-supported expected PRS signal capture than PGS000753 given the available fields.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (same trait_reported/trait_efo). However, PGS000753 is explicitly a *prevalent* AAA endpoint and is a very sparse P+T score (29 variants) with only a moderate OR per SD (1.37) and no PRS-comparable AUC/R2 reported. PGS003973 comes from a large disease-focused multi-cohort AAA GWAS meta-analysis and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with ~1.1M variants, which is structurally better supported for a polygenic disease when PRS-only metrics are absent. Its reported C-index (0.882) is full-model (age/age^2/sex) and thus not directly comparable as PRS performance, but it is at least based on basic covariates (no obvious clinical leakage) and the overall evidence package (study archetype + method/coverage) is stronger than the older sparse prevalent-endpoint score.

PGS002738 is the better-supported match to the target trait alcohol dependence because its endpoint is directly aligned: trait_efo is exactly "alcohol dependence" and both trait_reported/phenotyping_reported are "Alcohol use disorder" (a close clinical synonym). It also shows a strong discrimination signal via an OR(top 10% vs rest)=1.96 (1.54–2.51), which is meaningful PRS evidence even without PRS-only AUC/R2. In contrast, PGS000201 is less endpoint-faithful (trait_efo is "alcohol dependence measurement" and trait_reported is "Problematic alcohol use" with a DSM-5 criteria count phenotype), and its only PRS-comparable metric is a small incremental ΔR²=0.01192. Both lack PGS-only AUC/R², so the stronger endpoint fidelity plus stronger effect-size evidence favors PGS002738 despite its unknown covariates.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial fibrillation) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUC/C-index values are not directly comparable as PRS metrics. PGS005168’s reported discrimination (C-index 0.8718) is further compromised by explicit risk-wrapper covariates including the named clinical calculator CHARGE-AF (plus age/age^2/sex/array), which is a strong packaging/leakage signal that inflates full-model performance and weakens standalone PRS interpretability. PGS005313 uses only basic covariates (age, sex), avoiding that risk-calculator packaging, and it also has a strong per-SD effect size (OR 1.82) plus a more structurally rich cross-ancestry PRS-CSx genome-wide score (1,271,239 variants) with multi-ancestry evaluation context. Given cleaner covariates and stronger structural/effect-size support, PGS005313 is better-supported on the visible fields despite its lower full-model AUROC.

Both candidates map cleanly to the target (trait_efo = alcoholic liver cirrhosis), but PGS004913 has better endpoint fidelity in phenotyping_reported (Alcohol-associated liver cirrhosis matches the target) whereas PGS001777 uses a restricted/shifted endpoint ("Cirrhosis (males)") and has unknown covariates. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; PGS001777’s AUROC=0.671 is explicitly a full-model metric and thus not PRS-comparable, while PGS004913 at least provides an R²=0.029 and OR top vs bottom deciles=4.4 with clearly stated basic covariates (age, sex, 10 PCs), making its evidence cleaner and more interpretable. PGS004913 also uses more variants (20 vs 3) and has larger, explicitly described training/validation samples, supporting a more robust disease-focused PRS than the 3-variant score in PGS001777.

Both candidates map cleanly to the target (trait_efo = alcoholic liver cirrhosis), but PGS001777 comes from a disease-focused cirrhosis study and reports strong PRS-associated effect evidence (OR top 20% vs bottom 20% = 6.18; β=1.132), whereas PGS000704 appears to be a broader UKB framework score (biomarkers paper) with only a modest per-SD HR=1.18. Neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2 (both only show full-model discrimination: 0.671 vs 0.711, which is not PRS-comparable), so the decision rests mainly on endpoint/study focus and effect-size strength; PGS001777 is better supported on those. Confidence is low because PGS001777 has unknown covariates and a smaller validation sample, while PGS000704 has explicit basic covariates and larger training/validation.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial fibrillation). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model discrimination is not directly comparable; however PGS005168’s very high C-index (0.8718) is paired with explicit clinical risk-calculator packaging via CHARGE-AF in covariates, which strongly discounts its metric as PRS evidence. PGS002814 uses only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs), avoiding that leakage signal, and it provides stronger standalone PRS effect-size evidence (OR≈1.94 per SD vs PGS005168 HR≈1.67). Despite PGS005168 having a more genome-wide shrinkage method and many more variants, the CHARGE-AF packaging makes its reported performance less informative for PRS quality, so PGS002814 is better-supported on the visible fields.

PGS002755 is a closer match to the target trait as a general atopic eczema/atopic dermatitis endpoint (phenotyping_reported: incident atopic dermatitis), whereas PGS001773 targets a narrower subtype (moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis), which is a phenotype restriction relative to generic atopic eczema. Neither record provides PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUC/R2 are null for both); PGS001773’s very high AUROC=0.93 and R²=0.49 appear to be full-model metrics with covariates (including parental ethnicity) and are not comparable as standalone PRS evidence and are also implausibly high versus the eczema heritability ceiling, so they are discounted. With metrics not differentiating cleanly, structural evidence favors PGS002755’s genome-wide PRS-CS model with ~1.09M variants and large EUR evaluation (n=337,910) plus a reported HR (1.249 high vs low), over PGS001773’s 25-variant score with small validation (n=676).

PGS004587 is the better-supported match to the target trait (atopic eczema) because its endpoint is a direct, generic atopic dermatitis diagnosis framed as incident disease (“Incident atopic dermatitis”) and it reports a PRS-associated effect size (HR high vs low PRS = 1.153, 95% CI 1.037–1.282) in a very large European evaluation (n=337,910), with covariates that look like standard demographic/SES adjustments. In contrast, PGS001773 targets a narrower and potentially non-equivalent endpoint (“Moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis”) and its only strong-looking metrics (AUROC=0.93, R²=0.49) appear to be full-model/non-PRS-only and are therefore not comparable PRS performance; additionally, its covariates include parental ethnicity (family/ancestry packaging), and it has much smaller validation (n=676). With both lacking PRS-only AUC/R², the cleaner endpoint and more credible standalone PRS signal favor PGS004587.

Both candidates have good endpoint fidelity to the target (trait_efo=alcohol dependence; trait_reported/phenotyping_reported=Alcohol use disorder) and neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so we rely on structural and effect-size evidence. PGS002738 is a genome-wide PRS-CS score with very large variant count (326,000) and shows a slightly stronger reported discrimination signal (OR top 10% vs rest 1.96 [1.54–2.51]) than PGS002739 (OR 1.76 [1.32–2.34]), suggesting better stratification. PGS002739 is a gene-based PRS-CSx model with only 858 variants and AFR-only evaluation, which may limit general robustness; its added cross-ancestry method label doesn’t compensate for the much sparser model and weaker OR given the lack of PRS-only metrics. Confidence is moderate because both have unknown covariates and only OR-based performance reporting.

PGS005255 is less confounded by clinical covariate packaging and provides cleaner PRS evidence for aortic stenosis risk: it reports an HR per SD of 1.53 (with CI 1.40–1.66) using only basic covariates (age, age^2, sex, PCs), and its phenotyping_reported is incident aortic stenosis (aligned with the target despite trait_reported being a valve-function measure). In contrast, PGS005252 has an exact disease label/trait_efo match but its only discrimination metric is a full-model C-index/AUC=0.87 alongside a very heavy covariate set including multiple comorbidities (T2D, HTN, CAD, hyperlipidemia, renal failure, BMI, smoking), making that performance largely non-comparable to PRS-only quality; it also lacks CI for its HR. With no PGS-only AUC/R2 for either, the cleaner covariate design and interpretable effect-size evidence favor PGS005255.

PGS002739 is the better-supported match to the target trait alcohol dependence because its endpoint fidelity is direct: trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are both "Alcohol use disorder" and trait_efo is exactly "alcohol dependence." It also provides a clear case-control style discrimination signal (OR top 10% vs rest = 1.76, with CI), whereas PGS000201 is framed as "Problematic alcohol use" with an alcohol dependence measurement EFO and reports only a small incremental ΔR² (0.01192) plus a beta on a DSM-5 criteria count (log-transformed), which is a more quantitative/problem-use phenotype rather than a direct AUD diagnosis label. Although PGS000201 has cleaner disclosed covariates and a much larger genome-wide variant count, PGS002739’s closer phenotype alignment to alcohol dependence and its explicit risk stratification effect size outweigh the covariate-missingness penalty here.

PGS001263 is the better-supported choice for the target trait atrial flutter because it has exact endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Atrial flutter”) and it reports clean PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.617 and PGS-only R2=0.025), which can be sanity-checked against the provided heritability ceiling and interpreted without substituting covariate-boosted full-model AUROC. In contrast, PGS002050 uses a broader combined endpoint (“Atrial fibrillation and flutter”) rather than flutter-specific, and it lacks PRS-only AUROC/R2 entirely (only partial correlation is provided), making its predictive evidence less directly comparable for a flutter-specific selection despite larger variant count and training N.

PGS000327 has clean endpoint fidelity: trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to autism spectrum disorder, whereas PGS002790 has an explicit phenotype mismatch (phenotyping_reported = "Psychiatric behavior (withdrawn)") despite the ASD label fields. On PRS evidence, neither reports PGS-only AUC/R2, but PGS000327 provides a stronger disease-focused validation signal via an OR=1.33 per SD and a higher reported R² (0.0245) than PGS002790’s partial R²=0.00546, with similarly basic covariates. Given the primary importance of phenotype alignment plus stronger effect-size/performance support, PGS000327 is better-supported than PGS002790.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial fibrillation) and neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the reported AUROC values are full-model and not directly comparable as PRS metrics. Given that limitation, structural and transportability signals dominate: PGS005313 uses a genome-wide shrinkage cross-ancestry method (PRS-CSx) with far broader variant coverage (1,271,239 vs 4,520 for PGS002814’s P+T), and it is evaluated across multiple ancestries rather than only East Asian evaluation for PGS002814. Covariates are similarly light (age/sex for PGS005313; age/sex/PCs for PGS002814), so there’s no obvious covariate-leakage advantage for either. With comparable endpoint fidelity and no PRS-only metrics, the stronger method/variant architecture and broader evaluation support make PGS005313 better-supported overall.

Both candidates align to the target trait (atrial flutter) via the shared EFO mapping (atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter), but PGS001339 provides cleaner PRS-comparable performance evidence: it reports PGS-only AUROC=0.613 and PGS-only R2=0.02447 (no covariates), which can be sanity-checked against the provided heritability ceiling and is not reliant on full-model metrics. In contrast, PGS002050 lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R2 entirely and only reports partial correlation (partial-r=0.1034), making its predictive performance harder to compare and less directly interpretable as standalone PRS discrimination. Although PGS002050 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method with many more variants and slightly larger training N, the missing PRS-comparable metrics are a major evidence gap versus PGS001339’s explicit PGS-only results; both are UKB framework-style scores with similar endpoint wording, so the available PRS-only metrics tip the decision to PGS001339.

Both candidates are near-clones: identical trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (basal cell carcinoma), same publication, same EUR-only ancestry distribution, same training cohort (MGI) and training N (11,734), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), and same validation N (11,322). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC=0.632 is not a clean PRS-comparable differentiator. With endpoints and covariates effectively identical, the only visible edge is slightly stronger reported performance for PGS000454 (Nagelkerke R² 0.0489 vs 0.0487; top 1% vs rest OR 3.79 vs 3.61) while per-SD OR is essentially the same. This is a marginal advantage, hence low confidence.

PGS001263 is the better match to the target trait (atrial flutter) because its trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported are all specifically “Atrial flutter,” whereas PGS001339 is a combined endpoint (“Atrial fibrillation and flutter”) and explicitly time-to-event (phenotyping_reported: “TTE atrial fibrillation and flutter”), which is a weaker endpoint-fidelity fit for a generic atrial flutter target. Both are from the same pan-trait UKB sparse snpnet framework paper with identical training size, covariates, and validation N, so performance and design are directly comparable; on PRS-comparable metrics PGS001263 is also slightly higher (PGS-only AUROC 0.61716 vs 0.613; PGS-only R2 0.02517 vs 0.02447), with both remaining plausible under the heritability ceiling. Given near-identical context, the specific endpoint alignment plus marginally better PRS-only metrics favors PGS001263.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Disorders of bilirubin excretion” mapped to the same EFO), identical training cohort and size (UKB; n=391,124), identical covariates (basic demographics + PCs), identical ancestry evaluation mix, and essentially identical PRS-comparable performance evidence (partial-r=0.0716 with overlapping CIs). With metrics and phenotype effectively tied, the main differentiator is structural: PGS002032 is a genome-wide shrinkage score (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (19,768 variants) versus PGS001824’s very sparse penalized regression score (22 variants), which is generally less robust for polygenic signal capture absent contrary performance evidence. Therefore PGS002032 is better-supported on the visible fields.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to basal cell carcinoma (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and both use only basic covariates (age, sex, batch/PCs), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported—so full-model AUROC differences (0.632 for PGS000454 vs 0.64 for PGS000119) are not a clean PRS-comparable differentiator. PGS000454 has slightly stronger supporting evidence packaging on the visible record (reports additional metrics including Nagelkerke pseudo-R², Brier score, and top-1% OR=3.79) while maintaining a similar per-SD OR (1.661 vs 1.65) and similar training scale/ancestry context. PGS000119’s main advantages are marginally higher full-model AUROC and larger validation N, both weak signals here. Hence PGS000454 narrowly wins, but the lack of PRS-only metrics makes confidence low.

PGS002786 is the better match to the target trait (bipolar disorder): its trait_reported/trait_efo are exactly bipolar disorder, whereas PGS002788 targets the narrower subtype bipolar II disorder. Both candidates come from the same publication, use the same method (SDPR), have the same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, identical covariates (age, PCs1-3), and the same validation sample size (n=2,524), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only small partial R² values tied to non-disease phenotyping). Although PGS002788 has a slightly higher partial R² (0.00307 vs 0.00251), these are non-comparable full-model/partial metrics on different non-endpoint phenotypes and are too close to outweigh the endpoint-fidelity advantage of PGS002786.

Both candidates are essentially matched on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Breast cancer/breast carcinoma), study context (same publication), training cohort and size (UKB; n=12,483), evaluation ancestry mix (EUR/SAS), covariates (0), and validation sample size (n=48,968). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC/R² are only weak tie-breakers. On the visible metrics, PGS004153 is consistently slightly stronger than PGS004040 (full-model AUROC 0.6625 vs 0.6598; R² 0.0764 vs 0.0739; OR per SD 1.826 vs 1.809), and it also uses an ensemble MultiPRS approach (a positive structural signal vs a single-score LDpred2). The differences are small, hence moderate confidence.

Both candidates are near-clones in study context (same publication, SDPR method, PGC training cohort, EUR-only GWAS/EVAL, basic covariates age+PCs1-3) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R²—only a small partial R² (full-model/adjusted) that is not clearly PRS-comparable. Endpoint fidelity to the target trait “bipolar disorder” slightly favors PGS002787 because its mapped trait is bipolar I disorder (Type 1), which is closer to the generic bipolar disorder umbrella than PGS002788’s bipolar II disorder (Type 2), while both have noisy/non-diagnostic phenotyping_reported fields. PGS002788 has a marginally higher partial R² (0.00307 vs 0.00275) and slightly larger validation n, but these differences are tiny and not decisive given metric comparability limits, so the decision rests mainly on trait alignment.

Both candidates are near-clones: same breast cancer endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match), same publication/date, same variant count (1,041,298), same training cohort (UKB) and training N (12,483), same evaluation ancestry mix and validation N (48,968), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R² (only full-model AUROC/R² shown, which is not a clean PRS-comparable metric). With covariates listed as 0 for both, the only differentiator is marginally stronger reported full-model performance/effect sizes for PGS004040 (AUROC 0.6597897 vs 0.6597589; R² 0.073915 vs 0.073587; OR 1.8088 vs 1.8065), but the differences are tiny and likely noise—hence low confidence.

PGS000924 has clearly reported PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.88697 and PGS-only R²=0.21843) on a European validation record, whereas PGS001824 reports no PRS-only AUC/R² (only a modest partial correlation partial-r=0.0716), making its predictive support much weaker on the visible fields. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both, but PGS000924’s phenotype is a broader composite/time-to-event definition (“porphyrin and bilirubin metabolism (TTE)”), while PGS001824 is more directly aligned (“Disorders of bilirubin excretion”); this alignment advantage is outweighed by PGS000924’s much stronger and cleaner PRS-only metric reporting. Both are UKB-derived framework-style scores with basic covariates, so study archetype/covariate leakage does not differentiate them strongly here.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to celiac disease (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and neither reports PRS-comparable metrics (pgs_only_auc/pgs_only_r2 are null), so the listed AUROCs are full-model and not cleanly comparable. With that limitation, PGS000040 has a modest edge on structural evidence: it uses many more variants (228 vs 53 for PGS000316) and shows slightly higher reported AUROC (0.90 vs 0.879), while ancestry evaluation is clean EUR-only (vs PGS000316’s mixed/NR evaluation string). PGS000316’s much larger validation sample size is a weak tie-breaker and doesn’t overcome the lack of PRS-only metrics. Overall advantage to PGS000040, but confidence is low because both rely on full-model AUROC with unknown covariates.

Both candidates have perfect endpoint alignment to basal cell carcinoma (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and similarly clean/basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs), with EUR-only development/evaluation in MGI. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values (0.632 for PGS000452 vs 0.64 for PGS000119) are not strong differentiators. PGS000452 has slightly stronger supporting evidence on the visible record: it reports additional metrics (Nagelkerke pseudo-R²=0.0487, Brier score, and top-1% vs rest OR=3.61) beyond the per-SD OR (similar to PGS000119: 1.663 vs 1.65), making its performance characterization more complete/transparent. PGS000119’s larger validation N and slightly higher full-model AUROC are weak signals here. Overall edge to PGS000452, but near-tied hence low confidence.

Both candidates are essentially matched on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Breast cancer/breast carcinoma), study context (same publication), covariates (both listed as 0), training cohort and size (UKB; n=12,483), and ancestry distribution/evaluation (EUR with some SAS). Neither reports PRS-only AUROC/R², so the small full-model AUROC/R² differences are weak evidence. Given this near-tie, PGS004153 is preferred because it shows slightly stronger reported performance (full-model AUROC 0.6625 vs 0.6598; R² 0.0764 vs 0.0736; OR per SD 1.826 vs 1.806) and it is a MultiPRS/ensemble-style method, which is a positive structural signal over a single-score LDpred2-auto when other fields are equal.

PGS001301 has clearly reported PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.82867 and PGS-only R²=0.14224) with only basic covariates (age, sex, array, PCs), and it includes some non-EUR evaluation (AFR/SAS) in addition to EUR. In contrast, PGS000316 reports only a full-model AUROC (0.879) with unknown covariates and no PGS-only AUC/R², making its discrimination evidence non-comparable for PRS ranking despite a clean celiac endpoint label. Although PGS001301 comes from a pan-trait UKB framework paper (a penalty), the absence of PRS-only metrics for PGS000316 leaves weaker direct evidence of standalone PRS performance, so PGS001301 is better-supported on the visible fields.

PGS001301 is better supported on PRS-comparable evidence: it reports explicit PGS-only metrics (PGS AUROC(no covariates)=0.82867; PGS R2(no covariates)=0.14224) with only basic covariates (age, sex, array, PCs) and has broader evaluation ancestry (EUR plus AFR/SAS). PGS000040 has cleaner endpoint wording (Coeliac disease) but provides only a full-model AUROC=0.9 with unknown covariates and no PGS-only AUC/R2, making its performance less comparable for PRS quality ranking. Despite PGS001301 coming from a pan-trait UKB framework (a negative signal), the presence of PRS-only metrics and multi-ancestry evaluation outweighs PGS000040’s missing PRS-only evidence here.

PGS002786 is the better match to the target trait “bipolar disorder” at the concept level (trait_reported and trait_efo both map directly to bipolar disorder), whereas PGS002787 is explicitly subtype-restricted to bipolar I (trait_efo: bipolar I disorder). Neither record provides PRS-comparable performance (no PGS-only AUC/R2; only small partial R²/full_model_r2 values) and both come from the same publication, method (SDPR), EUR-only GWAS/EVAL, and similar covariates, so the slight partial R² advantage of PGS002787 is not a strong differentiator. Given the near-tie and both having non-disease phenotyping_reported fields, the direct trait alignment of PGS002786 breaks the tie.

PGS002032 is the better-supported choice for the target "bilirubin metabolism disease" because its endpoint is a direct match (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: "Disorders of bilirubin excretion" mapping cleanly to the target EFO) and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with substantial variant coverage (LDpred2; 19,768 variants), plus it is evaluated across multiple ancestries (AFR/EUR/GME/SAS), supporting portability. In contrast, PGS000924 comes from a pan-trait sparse UKB framework ("across 813 traits") with an explicitly broader/mixed endpoint (porphyrin + bilirubin; time-to-event), and an extremely sparse 5-variant model; although it reports strong-looking PRS-only AUROC/R², those metrics are less trustworthy here given the framework/TTE phenotype mismatch and the implausibly high PGS-only R² (0.218) relative to the provided heritability ceiling context (~0.089), suggesting non-comparability or scale mismatch. PGS002032 lacks PRS-only AUC/R², lowering confidence, but overall has cleaner phenotype fidelity and more credible PRS structure for this disease target than PGS000924.

Both candidates align well to the target trait (trait_efo=cervical carcinoma; trait_reported=Cervical cancer) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model C-index/AUROC is not a clean differentiator. On the visible evidence, PGS000073 has slightly stronger discrimination/effect evidence in its evaluation (C-index ~0.75; HR 1.22 [1.09–1.37]) than PGS005165 (C-index 0.566; HR 1.2 [1.06–1.36]), and PGS000073’s endpoint is explicitly incident cervical cancer. PGS005165 has more variants (15 vs 10) and is EAS-specific (useful for East Asian deployment), but its reported discrimination is materially lower and both are GWAS-hit style scores without PRS-only metrics. Therefore PGS000073 is better-supported overall on the record fields.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (ICD10 K80 cholelithiasis), same EFO mapping, same training cohort (UKB), same EUR-only development/evaluation, same variant count, and no PRS-comparable AUC/R2 reported—so performance must be judged from the available effect size. PGS004546 shows a higher per-SD odds ratio (OR=1.2986) than PGS004476 (OR=1.2194), indicating stronger PRS signal given otherwise near-clone metadata. Method differences (RFDiseasemetaPRS vs LDpred2) are secondary here because empirical metrics are sparse, but the higher OR supports PGS004546.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_efo cervical carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident cervical cancer; EUR evaluation). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher full-model AUROC/C-index in PGS000073 (0.745–0.75 vs 0.613) is not a clean PRS-comparable advantage, especially given PGS000073’s much heavier covariate set (PCs, parity, oral contraceptive use, pack-years, etc.) that can inflate full-model discrimination. PGS003428 is from a disease-focused cervical-phenotypes GWAS meta-analysis/risk stratification study and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred) with ~2.9M variants and a slightly stronger per-SD HR (1.33 vs 1.22), which is more indicative of PRS signal than covariate-augmented full-model AUROC. Overall, PGS003428 has the stronger structural PRS evidence and cleaner comparability despite the lower full-model metric.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_efo=cervical carcinoma; phenotyping is direct cervical cancer). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model C-index is only weakly informative; still, PGS003428 shows stronger discrimination/effect evidence (C-index 0.613; HR per SD 1.33) than PGS005165 (C-index 0.566; HR 1.2). Structurally, PGS003428 is a genome-wide LDpred score with ~2.9M variants from a cervical-phenotype GWAS meta-analysis context, whereas PGS005165 is a 15-SNP genome-wide-significant loci score from a pan-cancer risk paper, which is a weaker archetype and likely captures less polygenic signal. Covariates are acceptable in both (age/smoking vs basic demographics/PCs). Ancestry differs (EUR vs EAS), but with no deployment ancestry specified, the stronger disease-focused, genome-wide model with better effect/C-index evidence is preferred.

Both candidates are endpoint-aligned to corneal dystrophy (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported match), come from the same UKB portability paper, have identical training size, covariates, ancestry distribution, and validation sample size, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so we must rely on comparable PRS metrics and structural signals). PGS002042 shows stronger PRS-comparable performance via higher partial correlation (partial-r 0.0471 vs 0.0384 for PGS001835) and is a genome-wide score with far more variants (59,944 vs 38), which is generally a positive structural signal when other fields are effectively tied. Therefore PGS002042 is better supported on the visible evidence.

Both candidates map cleanly to cholelithiasis (same trait_efo), but PGS004476 has higher endpoint fidelity to the generic target via an ICD10 diagnosis definition (trait/phenotyping_reported: K80 cholelithiasis) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with ~1.06M variants, which is structurally more appropriate for a polygenic disease than the very sparse snpnet model in PGS001174 (970 variants) from a pan-trait UKB framework paper. PGS001174 does provide explicit PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.623, PGS-only R2 0.028) that are plausible vs the heritability ceiling, but its time-to-event endpoint (TTE) is a mild mismatch for a generic disease-risk target and its framework origin is a known generalization weakness. PGS004476 lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (only OR~1.22), so confidence is low, but the cleaner diagnosis endpoint plus stronger structural properties outweigh the modest PRS-only metrics from the sparse framework score.

PGS004621 is the better-supported match to the target trait (cirrhosis of liver): its trait_efo and phenotyping_reported are generic “Cirrhosis/cirrhosis of liver,” aligning directly with the umbrella endpoint, whereas PGS000704 is explicitly restricted to “Alcoholic cirrhosis” (trait_efo: alcoholic liver cirrhosis), a subtype mismatch for a generic cirrhosis target. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC/C-index (0.68 vs 0.711) is not a reliable differentiator; in that setting, PGS004621’s stronger per-SD effect size signal (OR 1.42 vs HR 1.18 for PGS000704) and its disease-focused multi-cohort development/validation context (multiple biobanks; very large EUR evaluation) outweigh PGS000704’s single-UKB development and subtype endpoint.

Both candidates match the target CAD endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all coronary artery disease) and both lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2, so selection leans on effect-size evidence, covariate cleanliness, and transportability. PGS003725 shows materially stronger reported PRS association (OR 2.14 and HR 1.75 per SD) than PGS002244 (OR 1.64 only), with similarly basic covariates (age/sex/PCs; PGS002244 adds possible dataset-specific technical covariates but no clear leakage). While PGS002244 has broader GWAS ancestry mix and more variants, those structural advantages are outweighed here by the stronger effect-size evidence for PGS003725 given the absence of PGS-only AUC/R2 for either model.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to COPD (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match), come from the same publication, use the same method (PRS-CS-auto), and are evaluated in EUR only, so the key differentiator is PRS-comparable performance. PGS001783 reports substantially higher PRS-only (covariates-regressed-out) Nagelkerke R2 (0.038092) than PGS001788 (0.0163), and also a slightly higher reported AUROC (0.74 vs 0.715), though AUROC is full-model and secondary. Both R2 values are plausible relative to the provided liability h2 ceiling (~0.0388), with PGS001783 essentially reaching that ceiling while remaining just below it, supporting stronger PRS signal. PGS001788 also uses a more complex covariate set (age2 and interaction terms) than PGS001783, making its full-model AUROC less directly interpretable, while still having weaker PRS-only R2. Therefore PGS001783 is better supported.

PGS002237 is better supported for the CKD target because it has higher endpoint fidelity and clearer disease-focused evidence: it specifies CKD stage 3+ with an explicit eGFR-based definition (<45 ml/min/1.73m2) and comes from a CKD-focused cross-ancestry prediction paper with multi-ancestry evaluation listed. It also reports a stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.47 vs 1.35 for PGS005113), which is the main comparable PRS signal available given that neither record provides PGS-only AUC/R2. PGS005113 has a method/variant-count advantage (PRS-CS; 1.1M variants) and cleaner/basic covariates, but it lacks training sample size information (N/A) and is embedded in a proteomics/T2D-comorbidities context with less CKD-specific endpoint detail, making its support for standalone CKD risk weaker on the visible fields.

ontology: congenital vitamin k-dependent coagulation factors deficiency
rationale: Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), identical training cohort and size (UKB; n=391,124), identical covariates (basic demographics + PCs), identical ancestry distribution and validation size (EUR eval; n=19,864), and essentially identical PRS-comparable performance evidence (partial-r 0.0563 for PGS002034 vs 0.0562 for PGS001826 with overlapping CIs). With metrics effectively tied and no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either, the main differentiator is structural: PGS002034 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (32,552 variants) versus PGS001826’s very sparse penalized regression model (45 variants). Given the same study context and near-identical observed performance, the higher-coverage shrinkage score is better-supported as a generalizable PRS.

Both candidates have good endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to cirrhosis). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC cannot be used as a comparable PRS metric (PGS004621’s AUROC=0.68 is full-model with age/sex/PCs). Given the lack of PRS-comparable metrics, structural/study-design signals dominate: PGS004621 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with ~1.09M variants and is developed/validated in a large multi-cohort biobank setting with basic covariates and very large EUR evaluation (n≈1.15M), which is generally more supportive for a polygenic disease than PGS000726’s 12-variant genome-wide-significant score. While PGS000726 reports a stronger tail-contrast OR (top 20% vs bottom 20% OR=2.26), it remains a very sparse model and has much smaller validation (n≈30k); overall the evidence package favors the genome-wide PRS-CS model.

Both candidates align to cholelithiasis (EFO match), but PGS004546 provides no PRS-comparable performance metrics (no PGS-only AUC/R2; only an OR≈1.30 and covariates listed as Unknown), making its predictive support hard to judge. PGS001174 reports clean PRS-only metrics in Europeans (PGS-only AUROC=0.623 and PGS-only R2=0.028), with basic covariates and values that are plausible relative to the trait’s h2_obs (~0.021), plus broader evaluation ancestry coverage. Despite being from a pan-trait UKB framework paper (a penalty), the explicit PRS-only performance evidence outweighs PGS004546’s largely missing metric support here.

PGS005090 is better supported for the target CKD endpoint because it is explicitly a CKD-focused study in Black American populations with fully aligned phenotype fields (CKD; stage 3+ is a clinically coherent CKD definition) and matched AFR GWAS/EVAL ancestry (100% African ancestry in both), improving transportability for non-EUR contexts. PGS005113 has a generic CKD label but comes from a proteomics/T2D-comorbidity framing paper, with EUR-only GWAS and mixed EUR/MAE evaluation, which is less directly CKD-focused and raises more concern that CKD is a secondary/comorbidity endpoint. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; PGS005090’s reported AUROC=0.9 is full-model and covariate-influenced (includes diabetes), so it cannot be used as PRS discrimination evidence, but PGS005090 still has slightly stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.41 vs 1.35) and a more disease-endpoint-focused validation context than PGS005113.

PGS001783 is better supported on PRS-comparable performance and structural signals for COPD: it reports a covariates-regressed-out/PRS-comparable Nagelkerke R2 of 0.0381, which is materially higher than PGS001332’s PGS-only R2 of 0.00235 and is consistent with the trait heritability ceiling guidance (h2_liability ~0.0388). Both candidates align to COPD at trait_reported/trait_efo, but PGS001783’s phenotyping_reported is an exact COPD endpoint, whereas PGS001332 uses a slightly broader ‘chronic obstructive airways disease/copd’ label. Study archetype also favors PGS001783: it comes from a global multi-biobank PRS-CS-auto framework with genome-wide coverage (884,139 variants) versus PGS001332’s pan-trait UKB ‘813 traits’ sparse snpnet score (482 variants), which domain guidance flags as often less reliable for external generalization despite having explicit PGS-only AUROC. Confidence is Moderate because PGS001783 lacks a PGS-only AUROC and has EUR-only evaluation, while PGS001332 has broader multi-ancestry evaluation records and explicit PGS-only AUROC (though low at 0.54).

Both candidates match the target trait (CKD stage ≥3) at the trait_reported/trait_efo level, but PGS002237 has clearer endpoint fidelity via phenotyping_reported (eGFR <45 ml/min/1.73m2, explicitly stage 3+), whereas PGS005090’s phenotyping_reported is vague (“Chronic kidney disease”). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so the full-model AUROC values (0.78 for PGS002237 vs 0.90 for PGS005090) are not comparable PRS metrics, especially given different covariate sets; PGS002237’s covariates are heavier (includes hypertension/diabetes/BMI/medication use), which further limits interpretability of its AUROC, but PGS005090 also lacks training sample size (N/A) and provides only a single performance record. With PRS-only metrics absent for both, PGS002237’s more specific phenotype definition plus multi-ancestry evaluation breadth (AFR/AMR/ASN/EUR/MAE) and reported OR (1.47) slightly outweigh PGS005090’s higher but likely covariate-inflated full-model AUROC and single-ancestry scope.

Both candidates match the target CAD endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Coronary artery disease”) and use only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs; PGS000013 also adds chip), so phenotype fidelity and leakage risk are similar. The key difference is PRS evidence quality: PGS003725 reports strong PRS effect sizes (HR 1.75 and OR 2.14 per SD with tight CIs) and comes from a disease-focused multi-ancestry CAD PRS study with explicitly diverse evaluation ancestries, supporting transportability. PGS000013 provides a PRS-comparable R2=0.04 (below the heritability ceiling, so plausible) but its prominent AUROC=0.81 is a full-model metric and not directly comparable as PRS performance; it also lacks effect-size evidence here. Given the stronger PRS-specific discrimination signal (OR/HR) plus multi-ancestry evaluation context, PGS003725 is better supported overall despite missing explicit PGS-only R2/AUC.

Both candidates align to the target COPD concept (trait_reported/trait_efo match), but PGS001788 has cleaner, stronger PRS-comparable signal and a more robust development context. PGS001788 reports a PRS-comparable Nagelkerke R2 with covariates regressed out of 0.0163, which is materially higher than PGS001332’s PGS R2 (no covariates) of 0.00235; both are below the COPD h2_obs ceiling (~0.0122) but PGS001788 is closer and thus more supportive of meaningful PRS contribution. PGS001332’s attractive-looking AUROC in the record is largely full-model (0.73063) with only a modest PGS-only AUROC (0.53971) and tiny incremental AUROC (0.003), consistent with covariate-driven discrimination rather than PRS strength. Study/design-wise, PGS001788 comes from a large multi-biobank global analysis with genome-wide shrinkage (PRS-CS-auto) and ~910k variants, whereas PGS001332 is a very sparse snpnet score (482 variants) from the pan-trait UKB ‘813 traits’ framework, which domain guidance flags as less reliable for external generalization. Although PGS001332 has some multi-ancestry evaluation listed, its PRS-only metrics are weak and its phenotyping_reported is slightly broader (‘chronic obstructive airways disease/copd’) than PGS001788’s direct COPD endpoint.

PGS000726 is the better-supported match to the target trait (cirrhosis of liver): its trait_efo and phenotyping_reported are generic “Cirrhosis/cirrhosis of liver,” aligning directly with the umbrella target, whereas PGS000704 is explicitly restricted to the subtype “Alcoholic cirrhosis” (trait_efo: alcoholic liver cirrhosis), which is a narrower endpoint mismatch for a generic cirrhosis target. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we rely on study/endpoint evidence and effect sizes: PGS000726 provides stronger PRS-linked effect evidence (OR top 20% vs bottom 20% = 2.26; per-SD OR=1.32) and comes from a disease-focused multi-cohort cirrhosis genetics study spanning multiple biobanks with multi-ancestry evaluation, while PGS000704 comes from a broad biomarker genetics UKB-only framework context and reports only a full-model C-index (0.711, not PRS-comparable) plus a modest per-SD HR=1.18. Overall, PGS000726 has cleaner endpoint fidelity and more directly interpretable PRS effect evidence than PGS000704.

Both candidates match the target CAD endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all coronary artery disease) and use similarly basic covariates (age/sex/PCs; PGS000013 also adds chip). The key differentiator is PRS evidence quality: PGS002244 provides a strong PRS effect size (OR per SD 1.64, 95% CI 1.61–1.67), which is a directly PRS-informative metric, and it has larger training (175,364 vs 120,280) and slightly larger validation (343,676 vs 288,978) with clear multi-ancestry evaluation. PGS000013 reports a PRS-only R2=0.04, but its prominent AUROC=0.81 is a full-model metric (not PRS-only) and thus not comparable as PRS discrimination evidence; overall its PRS signal evidence is not clearly stronger than the OR evidence in PGS002244. Given similar endpoint fidelity and covariates, the stronger PRS effect-size support and broader evaluation context favor PGS002244.

PGS003578 is better supported for the target depressive disorder because its endpoint is explicitly Major Depressive Disorder (Lifetime) with phenotyping_reported as major depressive disorder, matching the target disease concept at least as well as PGS002759’s broader “Depression” label. While neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R², PGS003578 provides a quantitative R² (0.0257) albeit as a generic/full-model metric, whereas PGS002759 provides only an OR (1.26 per SD), which indicates only modest PRS signal. PGS003578 also shows broader evaluation ancestry coverage (multi-ancestry EVAL) and clearer training context (UKB; n=67,164) than PGS002759 (training N/A, no cohorts listed), making its overall evidence package stronger despite the lack of clean PRS-only metrics in both.

PGS005170 is the better-supported match to the target trait dementia because its reported trait and EFO mapping align directly to dementia ("All-cause dementia"; trait_efo="dementia") with endpoint-consistent phenotyping (incident all-cause dementia), whereas PGS000823 is primarily an Alzheimer’s disease score (trait_efo="Alzheimer disease"), making it a subtype/partial match for a generic dementia target despite similar phenotyping text. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we rely on structural and design signals: PGS005170 uses an explicit multi-score integrative/ensemble approach with genome-wide coverage (~1.32M variants) and shows a per-SD HR=1.25, while PGS000823 is a sparse 23-variant genome-wide-significant score with only a grouped HR (top vs bottom tertile) and less PRS-isolated evidence. PGS005170’s covariates include APOE ε2/ε4 dosage (a mild comparability concern), but PGS000823’s simpler covariates do not compensate for its weaker endpoint alignment and much sparser model.

Both candidates align well to the target (trait_efo = major depressive disorder; phenotyping_reported is a direct depression/MDD endpoint) and are EUR-only in GWAS and evaluation, so endpoint and ancestry do not separate them. The key differentiator is performance evidence: PGS002759 reports a PRS effect size (OR per SD = 1.26, 95% CI 1.22–1.30), which is a PRS-comparable signal of discriminative strength, whereas PGS003333 reports only a Nagelkerke pseudo-R2 of 0.022 that appears to be a full-model/unspecified metric (no PGS-only R2/AUC) and has unknown covariates, making the metric harder to interpret as PRS-only. Methods/variant counts are essentially similar (PRS-CS vs PRS-CS-auto; ~1.09M variants) and validation N differences are minor, so the clearer PRS-specific effect size evidence favors PGS002759.

PGS000997 is better supported on PRS-comparable evidence: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC (0.591) and PGS-only R² (0.0178) with only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs, array), making the performance interpretable as standalone PRS signal and consistent with the trait’s low heritability ceiling. In contrast, PGS004614 reports only a full-model AUROC (0.76) with covariates including family history (a clinical augmentation that inflates and makes AUROC non-comparable) and provides no PGS-only AUC/R² or effect sizes; its training sample size is also missing. Although PGS004614 is disease-focused and genome-wide (many variants), the lack of PRS-only metrics plus family-history packaging makes its visible support weaker than PGS000997’s clean PRS-only reporting.

Both candidates are from the same Nat Genet study, use the same method (PRS-CS), and target the same EFO trait with the same reported trait label (Dilated cardiomyopathy (MTAG)), so the decision hinges on endpoint fidelity and PRS-only evidence. PGS004951 uses a direct clinical DCM phenotype ("Clinical dilated cardiomyopathy") with lighter covariates (sex, PC1-12) and shows a larger PRS contribution (delta liability-scale R^2 0.101; delta Nagelkerke 0.076) than PGS004949 (0.095 and 0.029), with similar per-SD OR (~1.93 vs 1.91). Although PGS004949 has a slightly higher PRS-only AUC (0.68 vs 0.67) and much larger validation N, its phenotype is narrower ("Non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy") and its covariate set is heavier (age, age^2, array), and its reported AUPRC is extremely low (0.0052 vs 0.2023), making its apparent advantage less convincing on the visible PRS-only contribution. Therefore PGS004951 is better-supported for generic dilated cardiomyopathy risk.

PGS004614 is the better-supported choice for diverticular disease because it is disease-focused with exact endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Diverticular disease”) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (SBayesR) with very large variant coverage (1,082,282), plus multi-ancestry evaluation is indicated (AFR/EUR/SAS). Although its only visible AUROC (0.76) is a full-model metric and is likely inflated by inclusion of family history (covariates include family history, age, sex), PGS000996’s advantage of reporting PRS-only metrics is weak: it comes from a pan-trait UKB framework (“across 813 traits”), is very sparse (368 variants), and shows low PRS-only performance (PGS-only AUROC 0.5519; PGS-only R2 0.00372). Overall, PGS004614’s disease-specific study context and stronger structural properties outweigh PGS000996’s modest PRS-only metrics from a framework sparse model.

Both candidates are essentially matched on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported for Dupuytren contracture), study context (same UKB portability paper), training size (n=391,124), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), ancestry distribution, and validation size (n=18,971). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; both only provide a similar partial correlation (PGS002092 partial-r=0.0797 vs PGS001880 partial-r=0.0783), which is a negligible difference. With metrics and phenotype effectively tied, the main differentiator is structural: PGS002092 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far more variants (484,484 vs 2,443), which is generally favored for polygenic traits when other evidence is comparable.

Both candidates target the same trait (Dilated cardiomyopathy (MTAG); EFO matches) and use the same method (PRS-CS) with broadly comparable, non-leaky covariates (A: age/sex/PCs; B: sex/PCs). The key differentiator is that PGS004951 reports PRS-comparable performance (explicit univariate PRS-only AUC=0.67 with CI and delta PRS/residual liability-scale R²=0.101), plus a stronger per-SD OR (1.93 vs 1.76) and a substantially larger variant set (1,075,760 vs 709,534), all supporting stronger standalone PRS signal. PGS004862 lacks any PRS-only AUC/R² and only provides full-model AUROC/R² (0.71/0.05), which is not comparable as PRS evidence despite its larger validation sample size.

PGS005170 is the better-supported match to the target trait dementia because its endpoint is explicitly aligned (trait_reported: all-cause dementia; phenotyping_reported: incident all-cause dementia; trait_efo: dementia) and it is structurally stronger as an ensemble/integrative PRS (24 component PRSs; 1,320,229 variants) with multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR). Although it only reports a full-model AUROC (0.761) and an HR=1.25 and includes APOE allele dosage as a covariate (making the AUROC not PRS-comparable), it still avoids the larger phenotype mismatch present in PGS002249, which is labeled Alzheimer’s disease (trait_efo: Alzheimer disease) rather than dementia overall. PGS002249 also lacks PRS-comparable metrics (only a high-vs-low HR=1.91, not per-SD) and uses lifestyle-category covariates that suggest risk-factor packaging, reducing comparability for standalone PRS assessment despite its much larger validation sample (n=196,383).

Both candidates align well to the target (trait_efo=major depressive disorder; phenotyping_reported is MDD in both), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R² (so the listed R² values are not clean PRS-comparable). Given that, structural/transportability evidence dominates: PGS003578 has broader evaluation ancestry (AFR/AMR/ASN/EAS/EUR rather than EUR-only for PGS003333) and a slightly higher reported R² (0.0257 vs 0.022) under explicitly basic covariates (PCs 1–10), whereas PGS003333 has unknown covariates and EUR-only evaluation. Although PGS003333 is trained from multiple cohorts (23andMe/PGC/UKB) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage method, the lack of PRS-only metrics and unknown covariates make its support less clean than PGS003578’s explicitly adjusted, multi-ancestry evaluation package.

Both candidates map to Alzheimer’s disease (trait_reported/trait_efo) and neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2, so we rely on endpoint fidelity, covariate cleanliness, and effect-size evidence. PGS002249 has phenotyping_reported = incident dementia, which aligns directly with the target trait (dementia), and shows a stronger risk gradient (HR 1.91 high vs low) than PGS000823 (HR 1.36 top vs bottom tertile). PGS000823’s phenotyping_reported is incident all-cause dementia (also aligned) and uses cleaner covariates (age/sex only), but its much smaller variant set (23 GWAS hits) and weaker HR provide less support for a robust dementia-risk PRS than PGS002249’s genome-wide clumped score (249,273 variants) with stronger observed association, despite PGS002249’s heavier lifestyle/SES covariate adjustment making its reported HR somewhat less PRS-isolated.

Both candidates align well to the target (same EFO: Dupuytren Contracture; phenotyping_reported is a direct Dupuytren/contracture diagnosis in both). PGS001254 is better supported on PRS-comparable performance evidence: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC=0.6646 and PGS-only R²=0.0247 (with CIs for AUROC), whereas PGS001880 provides no PRS-only AUROC/R² and only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0783), which is harder to compare and less directly interpretable as discrimination. Although PGS001880 has broader multi-ancestry evaluation and many more variants (2443 vs 11), the lack of standard PRS-only metrics makes its predictive strength less evidenced on the record than PGS001254’s clearly reported PRS-only metrics.

PGS000997 is better supported for the target trait (diverticular disease) because it has cleaner and stronger PRS-comparable performance on the selected European validation: higher PGS-only AUROC (0.591 vs 0.552) and higher PGS-only R2 (0.0178 vs 0.0037). Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both, but PGS000997 maps directly to diverticular disease of intestine (time-to-event) with trait_efo exactly “diverticular disease,” whereas PGS000996 mixes “diverticular disease/diverticulitis” and trait_efo includes diverticulitis (slightly broader/less specific). Both come from the same pan-trait UKB snpnet framework with identical training cohort, covariates, and ancestry setup, so the decisive differentiator is the materially stronger PRS-only metrics and larger variant set for PGS000997 (5757 vs 368), with its PRS-only R2 also remaining below the heritability ceiling sanity-check.

Both candidates target dilated cardiomyopathy with the same reported trait label “Dilated cardiomyopathy (MTAG)” and use the same method (PRS-CS) with only basic demographic/PC covariates, so neither shows obvious clinical-risk packaging. Candidate B (PGS004949) provides cleaner PRS-comparable performance evidence: it explicitly reports a univariate (PRS-only) AUC=0.68 (with CI) and PRS delta R² metrics, whereas candidate A (PGS004862) reports only full-model AUROC=0.71 and R²=0.05 (not PRS-only), which is not comparable per the guidance. Although PGS004949’s phenotyping_reported is slightly narrower (“Non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy”) and its evaluation ancestry is MAE-only (vs EUR-only for PGS004862), the presence of explicit PRS-only metrics plus a slightly stronger OR (1.91 vs 1.76) makes PGS004949 better-supported overall on the visible fields.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target (trait_efo=follicular lymphoma; trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Nodular lymphoma”), from the same publication, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same training (n=3,696) and validation size (n=3,256), and same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences are weak. On the visible metrics, PGS000644 has slightly higher AUROC (0.538 vs 0.532) and slightly higher pseudo-R² (0.00349 vs 0.00282) and OR per SD (1.149 vs 1.133), while PGS000643 only stands out on the top-1% vs rest OR (2.49 vs 1.48). Given the otherwise identical design and lack of PRS-only metrics, the small but consistent edge in overall discrimination/effect size favors PGS000644, though the evidence is close.

PGS002304 is the cleaner endpoint match to the target: trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are both explicitly “Follicular lymphoma,” whereas PGS000643 is labeled/phenotyped as “Nodular lymphoma” despite mapping to the follicular lymphoma EFO, creating endpoint-fidelity ambiguity. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values (0.61 for PGS002304 vs 0.532 for PGS000643) are not strongly comparable; PGS000643 does at least report PRS-associated effect sizes and Nagelkerke R², but these are still not clearly PRS-only and come with basic covariates. Given the primary importance of phenotype alignment and the lack of clean PRS-only metrics for both, PGS002304 edges out on endpoint fidelity, but confidence is low because PGS002304 has unknown covariates and much smaller validation (n=197) while PGS000643 has larger validation and richer metric reporting.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (same trait_efo Dupuytren Contracture; phenotyping_reported is a direct Dupuytren/contracture diagnosis in both). PGS001254 reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.6646; PGS R2 0.0247), whereas PGS002092 lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R2 and only shows a partial correlation (partial-r 0.0797), so metric evidence favors PGS001254. However, PGS002092 has materially stronger structural/portability support: a genome-wide LDpred2 score with 484,484 variants (vs 11 variants for the sparse snpnet score) and evaluation across multiple ancestries (AFR/EUR/GME/SAS), while PGS001254 is a pan-trait sparse UKB framework score evaluated only in EUR—an archetype that domain guidance flags as less reliable for external generalization. Given comparable phenotype fidelity, the stronger method/coverage and multi-ancestry evaluation make PGS002092 better-supported overall despite missing PRS-only AUROC/R2.

PGS002304 has the cleanest endpoint fidelity to the target: trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are both explicitly “Follicular lymphoma” (trait_efo also matches), whereas PGS000644 is labeled/phenotyped as “Nodular lymphoma” despite mapping to follicular lymphoma in trait_efo, creating a clearer phenotype-label mismatch. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values are not strong PRS-comparable differentiators; still, PGS002304’s reported AUROC (0.61) is higher than PGS000644’s (0.538). PGS000644 does have more transparent basic covariates and reports additional metrics/effect sizes, but its PRS signal looks weak (Nagelkerke R² 0.00349; OR per SD ~1.15) and the phenotype mismatch weighs more heavily for this target. Overall, PGS002304 is better supported primarily on endpoint alignment, with moderate confidence due to both lacking PRS-only metrics and PGS002304 having unknown covariates and small validation n.

Both candidates have identical endpoint alignment to Hashimoto’s thyroiditis (trait_efo) with the same reported/phenotyped label (“lymphocytic thyroiditis”), same publication family, same evaluation ancestry mix, and same validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not a clean PRS-comparable metric). With metrics essentially non-differentiating, structural/effect-size evidence breaks the tie: PGS005271 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRSCS) with ~1.09M variants and shows a much stronger per-SD effect size (OR≈1.55) than PGS005270’s very sparse P+T score (55 variants) with near-null effect (OR≈1.04). The small full-model AUROC edge for PGS005270 (0.639 vs 0.630) is likely noise and not sufficient to outweigh PGS005271’s stronger PRS signal and more polygenic construction.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target (trait_efo=Hashimoto's thyroiditis; trait_reported/phenotyping_reported=lymphocytic thyroiditis), same method (PRSCS), same evaluation ancestry mix, same validation sample size (n=94,651), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC is shown, which is discounted). With endpoint and design essentially tied, PGS005271 has consistently stronger visible performance/effect evidence than PGS005272: higher full-model AUROC (0.6297 vs 0.6054) and higher per-SD effect sizes (OR 1.55 vs 1.42; beta 0.438 vs 0.349). PGS005271 also lists a slightly broader set of development cohorts (includes BBJ and MVP), though this is a weak tie-break. Overall, PGS005271 is better-supported on the available fields.

Both candidates target the same endpoint with identical trait_efo (Hashimoto's thyroiditis) and phenotyping_reported (lymphocytic thyroiditis), come from the same publication, and have the same evaluation ancestry mix and validation sample size (n=94,651), with covariates unknown for both—so endpoint fidelity and transportability context are essentially tied. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; the only AUROC shown is full-model and not a clean PRS-comparable metric, and the small full-model AUROC advantage of PGS005270 (0.639 vs 0.605) is not decisive. Under the fallback when PGS-only metrics are absent, PGS005272 is better supported structurally and by effect size: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRSCS) with far more variants (1,085,142 vs 55) and shows a much stronger per-SD OR (1.42 vs 1.04), indicating materially stronger PRS signal than PGS005270’s sparse P+T score.

Both candidates map cleanly to the target concept (trait_reported/trait_efo are hip osteoarthritis). However, PGS002763 has better endpoint fidelity for a generic “hip osteoarthritis” target because its phenotyping_reported is simply “Hip osteoarthritis,” whereas PGS004882 is explicitly “Incident hip osteoarthritis,” a time-to-event/incident-only framing that is a mild mismatch for a generic disease-risk target. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we rely on effect-size evidence and design cleanliness: both show similar per-SD effects (PGS002763 OR=1.38 vs PGS004882 HR=1.4), but PGS004882’s only discrimination metric is a full-model C-index=0.6 (not PRS-comparable) and it comes from an absolute-incidence framework paper, while PGS002763 avoids that packaging signal and uses only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/technical). Overall, PGS002763 is the cleaner, more directly aligned PRS record on the visible fields.

PGS002763 has the cleaner endpoint match to the target trait: phenotyping_reported is explicitly “Hip osteoarthritis,” whereas PGS002728 uses “Total hip replacement,” a treatment/proxy endpoint that can reflect access/clinical decision factors beyond disease status. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS002728’s reported AUROC=0.66 is a full-model metric (age, sex) and not a comparable standalone PRS metric; by contrast PGS002763 at least provides a PRS effect size (OR=1.38 per SD), giving direct evidence of PRS signal. Structurally, PGS002763 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with ~1.05M variants versus 44 GWAS hits for PGS002728, which is generally more appropriate for a polygenic trait like hip osteoarthritis. Both are EUR-only in GWAS/EVAL; PGS002728 has multi-cohort development listed, but the endpoint mismatch and lack of PRS-comparable metrics outweigh that advantage.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity for the target (trait_efo=Hodgkins lymphoma; phenotyping_reported and trait_reported both Hodgkin's disease), identical ancestry context (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), identical training cohort (MGI) and training/validation sizes (n=736 train; n=775 eval), and similarly clean/basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences are only weakly informative; still, PGS000639 shows consistently stronger validation signals than PGS000638: higher AUROC (0.62 vs 0.601), higher pseudo-R² (0.0276 vs 0.0193), higher OR per SD (1.476 vs 1.377), and higher top-1% vs rest OR (2.64 vs 1.62). With otherwise near-clone metadata, these stronger effect-size/performance indicators make PGS000639 better supported.

PGS002728 is better supported for the target trait because it comes from a disease-focused OA risk assessment study with multi-cohort development (EB, GARP, HUNT, LLS, MyCode, UKB, arcOGEN, deCODE) and uses only basic covariates (age, sex), whereas PGS004882 is from a broad multi-disease incidence framework paper and is developed on a minimal cohort context (1000G listed; samples_training n=404), which is a weaker study archetype signal despite its huge evaluation N. Neither record reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model metrics are not cleanly comparable; the small full-model discrimination difference (0.66 AUROC for PGS002728 vs 0.60 C-index for PGS004882) is secondary. Endpoint-wise, PGS002728 uses total hip replacement (a treatment/proxy endpoint) while PGS004882 uses incident hip OA (more direct), but the framework penalty and weaker development evidence for PGS004882 outweigh that advantage, making PGS002728 the stronger overall choice on visible metadata.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target hyperthyroidism via the clinically dominant subtype Graves’ disease: identical trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported, same method (PRSCS), same evaluation ancestry mix (MAE 100%) and same validation sample size (n=94,651), with covariates unknown in both and no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported (only full-model AUROC, which is not PRS-comparable). With endpoint fidelity and study context effectively tied, the only differentiators are small performance/effect-size differences: PGS005265 has slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.6652 vs 0.6637) and stronger per-SD effect sizes (OR 1.625 vs 1.543; β 0.486 vs 0.434), plus a trivially higher variant count. These are modest, hence low confidence, but they favor PGS005265.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported = Hodgkin's disease; trait_efo = Hodgkins lymphoma), identical ancestry context (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), same training cohort (MGI) and training/validation sizes (n=736 train; n=775 eval), and similarly clean/basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use PRS-comparable metrics and must treat the full-model AUROC as only weakly informative. Within this like-for-like setting, PGS000639 shows consistently stronger observed performance/effect evidence than PGS000637: higher AUROC (0.62 vs 0.574), higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0276 vs 0.013), and higher per-SD OR (1.476 vs 1.3). Despite PGS000637 using many more variants (PRS-CS genome-wide), its reported discrimination is weaker here, so PGS000639 is better supported on the visible validation results.

Both candidates are near-clones: same target trait_efo and phenotyping_reported (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), same method (PRS-CS), same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same covariates (age, age^2, sex, PC1-10), same development cohorts, and same validation sample size. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC/R² are not clean PRS-comparable metrics; however, within this identical covariate/endpoint setting, PGS004911 shows consistently stronger reported performance/effect evidence than PGS004910 (AUROC 0.80 vs 0.73; R² 0.048 vs 0.031; HR 2.34 vs 1.97; OR per SD 1.33 vs 1.26; high-vs-median tertile OR 5.9 vs 5.5). Additionally, PGS004911 is the MTAG-enhanced version, which domain guidance mildly prefers over the base model when endpoints are aligned. Therefore PGS004911 is better supported on the visible fields.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match disorders of iron metabolism), identical training cohort and size (UKB, n=391,124), identical covariates (basic demographics + PCs), and identical multi-ancestry evaluation distribution and validation N (n=19,883), so the decision rests on comparable PRS signal and structural properties. PGS002031 shows slightly higher PRS-comparable performance (partial-r 0.1355 vs 0.1307 for PGS001823) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with a much larger variant set (6713 vs 654), which is a positive structural signal when other fields are effectively tied. The metric difference is small, so confidence is moderate rather than high.

PGS005266 is better supported for the target hyperthyroidism because its endpoint (phenotyping_reported/trait_reported = Graves’ disease) is a clinically dominant cause of hyperthyroidism and comes from a disease-focused, multi-cohort biobank study context with broad external validation ancestry listed (African American or Afro-Caribbean, Hispanic/Latin American, European) and a large validation sample (n=94,651). It also reports a strong PRS effect size (OR≈1.54 per SD), which is meaningful evidence of PRS discrimination even though PRS-only AUC/R2 are not provided (only a full-model AUROC ~0.664, which is not PRS-comparable). In contrast, PGS001043 has exact label alignment (hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis) and does report clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.6323; PGS R2=0.0216, below the heritability ceiling), but it is from the known pan-trait UKB “813 traits” sparse snpnet framework with very low variant count (69) and single-biobank development, which is a negative transportability/study-archetype signal versus the disease-focused multi-cohort design of PGS005266. Overall, the stronger disease-focused evidence package and effect size support PGS005266 despite missing PRS-only AUC/R2.

PGS001320 is better-supported on PRS-comparable evidence: it reports explicit PGS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.629 and PGS-only R²=0.06493) with basic covariates (age, sex, array, PCs), enabling a clean assessment of PRS contribution and passing the heritability-ceiling sanity check (R² well below h2_liability~0.36). In contrast, PGS004234 provides only a full-model AUROC (0.763) with a heavier covariate set (including smoking and BMI) and no PGS-only AUROC/R² or effect sizes, so its apparent performance is likely covariate-driven and not comparable as standalone PRS evidence. Both match the hypertension endpoint, but the stronger, PRS-isolated metric reporting makes PGS001320 the more defensible choice despite its framework-paper origin.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity for the target (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported = Hodgkin's disease; trait_efo = Hodgkins lymphoma), identical ancestry context (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), same training cohort (MGI) and training/validation sizes (n=736 train; n=775 eval), and similarly basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either (so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative). Given this near-clone setup, PGS000638 is favored because it shows consistently slightly stronger reported performance/effect evidence in the selected validation record (full-model AUROC 0.601 vs 0.574; Nagelkerke R² 0.0193 vs 0.013; per-SD OR 1.377 vs 1.30). PGS000637’s much larger variant count/method (PRS-CS, 1,047,511 variants) is a structural plus, but within this same-publication/same-endpoint comparison the only visible empirical discrimination signals are modestly better for PGS000638, so it wins with low confidence.

PGS004236 is from a hypertension-focused multi-ethnic study with multi-cohort development (BioMe, MVP, UKB) and explicitly multi-ancestry evaluation, and it reports a strong PRS effect size (OR=2.1) consistent with meaningful standalone signal. Although it lacks PRS-only AUROC/R² (only a full-model AUROC=0.764, which is not PRS-comparable and is further confounded by heavier covariates including BMI and smoking), PGS001320’s main advantage is simply having PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.629, R²=0.0649) but it comes from the known pan-trait UKB “813 traits” sparse framework (snpnet) with EUR-only development and modest PRS-only discrimination. Given domain guidance that disease-focused multi-cohort scores typically outperform pan-trait sparse UKB framework scores unless the framework has clearly superior endpoint+metric evidence, PGS004236 is better-supported overall despite missing PRS-only AUC/R².

Both candidates target the same trait (hypertension; EFO hypertension) with the same reported phenotype (“Prevelant hypertension”), identical covariates (age/age^2/sex/PCs plus smoking and BMI), same training N (10,314) and same validation size (39,035), and both only report full-model AUROC (~0.763–0.764) with no PGS-only AUC/R2—so the AUROC difference is essentially noise and not PRS-comparable. The key differentiator is that PGS004236 provides stronger PRS-specific evidence via an effect size (OR=2.1 per SD, 95% CI 1.99–2.21), while PGS004234 reports no effect sizes at all, leaving less direct support for standalone PRS discrimination. PGS004236 also has broader development cohort listing (BioMe, MVP, UKB vs BioMe, UKB) and a higher variant count (398,805 vs 234,228), which mildly supports capturing more polygenic signal given otherwise matched endpoints.

Both candidates match the target trait (trait_reported/trait_efo = hypothyroidism). However, PGS005218 is from a disease-focused hypothyroidism GWAS/prediction study with multi-cohort development (23andMe, FinnGen, UKB, deCODE, etc.) and a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS; 1,110,091 variants), which is structurally more appropriate for a polygenic disease than the sparse SnpNet score in PGS004935 (6,127 variants) from a portability-style paper and single-cohort UKB development.
