Performance-wise, neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; PGS005218’s higher full-model AUROC (0.859) is not directly comparable and is heavily covariate-inflated by thyroid biomarkers (TSH, T4, anti-TPO), but PGS004935’s full-model AUROC is lower (0.7) and its covariates are unknown, offering no cleaner comparability advantage. Given the stronger study archetype and genome-wide construction despite covariate concerns, PGS005218 is better-supported overall.

PGS000114 is the better match to the target trait (juvenile idiopathic arthritis): its trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported are all the umbrella JIA endpoint, whereas PGS000325 is explicitly for the oligoarticular JIA subtype (endpoint mismatch for a generic JIA target). Both candidates come from the same disease-focused publication, use the same method (SparSNP), have the same basic covariates (sex, PCs 1–10), and are EUR-only in development/evaluation, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC), so the higher full-model AUROC for PGS000325 (0.80 vs 0.738) is discounted and does not outweigh endpoint fidelity. Effect sizes are similarly strong (OR 2.085 for PGS000114 vs 1.93 for PGS000325), leaving phenotype alignment as the main differentiator.

Both candidates match the target trait well (trait_reported/trait_efo are hypothyroidism). However, PGS005218’s only visible discrimination is a full-model AUROC=0.859 while using heavy near-outcome thyroid biomarkers (TSH, T4, anti-TPO) as covariates, making that AUROC largely non-comparable and not good evidence of standalone PRS quality (and no PGS-only AUC/R2 is provided). PGS002766, while also lacking PGS-only AUC/R2, provides a PRS effect size (OR per SD=1.47, 95% CI 1.43–1.52) under basic covariates (age, sex, PCs, technical), which is cleaner and more directly attributable to the PRS. Given the covariate-leakage concern in PGS005218 and the presence of a reasonably strong PRS OR in PGS002766, PGS002766 is better-supported on the visible fields.

PGS005265 is better supported for the target hyperthyroidism because its endpoint (Graves’ disease) is the clinically dominant autoimmune cause of hyperthyroidism and is explicitly diagnosed in phenotyping_reported, whereas PGS001043 is a pan-trait UKB framework score (“across 813 traits”) that is known to generalize less well despite an exact-label match. Although PGS001043 reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.6323; PGS R2 0.02158, below the h2 ceiling) with basic covariates, PGS005265 provides stronger disease-focused multi-cohort development/validation context (many biobanks; multi-ancestry evaluation) and a strong per-SD effect size (OR 1.63), while PGS001043 is extremely sparse (69 variants) and trained only in UKB—both warning signals for portability. Confidence is moderate because PGS005265 lacks PRS-only AUROC/R2 (only full-model AUROC shown), making the performance comparison less direct.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_efo and phenotyping_reported are hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), but PGS004911 is better-supported as a standalone PRS: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with 374,114 variants versus PGS000739’s 27 genome-wide significant variants, which is structurally more appropriate for capturing polygenic signal. Performance reporting is imperfect for both (no PGS-only AUC/R2), but PGS004911’s reported effect sizes (OR per SD 1.33; HR 2.34; OR high vs median tertile 5.9) provide direct PRS signal evidence under only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs), whereas PGS000739’s AUROC=0.821 is a full-model metric with heavy clinical covariates (multiple comorbid risk factors plus rare-variant carrier status), making its discrimination less attributable to the PRS and less comparable. Validation size differences (343k vs 185k) are secondary here.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all hypertrophic cardiomyopathy). However, PGS000739’s reported AUROC=0.821 is a full-model metric with heavy clinical covariates (obesity, HTN, AF, CAD) plus rare-variant carrier status, making the discrimination largely non-comparable to a standalone PRS and raising leakage/packaging concerns. PGS004910 also only reports full-model metrics (AUROC=0.73, R²=0.031), but uses much cleaner covariates (age, age^2, sex, PC1-10) and provides PRS-relevant effect sizes (HR 1.97; OR per SD 1.26; OR high vs median tertile 5.5) alongside a genome-wide shrinkage construction (PRS-CS; 374,190 variants) versus a sparse 27-variant GWS score. With no PGS-only AUC/R² available for either, the cleaner covariate design and stronger polygenic construction make PGS004910 better-supported than the clinically augmented PGS000739.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Hypothyroidism”) and are EUR-trained/EUR-evaluated in UKB, with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either. PGS004935 reports an AUROC=0.7, but it is explicitly a full-model/classification metric (not PRS-only) and covariates are “Unknown,” so that AUROC is not comparable evidence of standalone PRS quality. With comparable endpoint fidelity and similarly strong per-SD effect sizes (PGS002766 OR=1.47 vs PGS004935 OR=1.5), the stronger structural signal favors PGS002766: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with far broader variant coverage (1,092,122 vs 6,127), whereas PGS004935 is a sparse SnpNet score from a portability-framed paper. Validation size differences are a weak tie-break and don’t outweigh the above.

Both candidates are from the same disease-focused publication, use the same method (SparSNP), have similar basic covariates (sex, PCs 1–10), and are EUR-only in development/evaluation, so endpoint fidelity and transportability are broadly comparable (both are JIA subtypes rather than generic JIA). With no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either (only full-model AUROC, which is discounted), the best differentiators are the available discrimination/effect-size signals and structural support: PGS000325 shows higher AUROC (0.80 vs 0.76) and a materially stronger per-SD OR (1.93 vs 1.51), and it also uses more variants (21 vs 12). Training/validation sample sizes are very similar and not decisive. Therefore PGS000325 is better supported than PGS000326 on the visible evidence.

PGS000114 is the better match to the target trait (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) because its trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported are all the umbrella JIA endpoint, whereas PGS000326 is explicitly a subtype score (RF-negative polyarticular JIA) and thus has weaker endpoint fidelity for a generic JIA target. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2 (both only show full-model AUROC), so the small AUROC difference (0.738 vs 0.76) is not a reliable differentiator. With otherwise similar study context (same publication, method, cohorts, EUR-only), PGS000114 also has a stronger reported effect size (OR 2.085 vs 1.51) and more variants (26 vs 12), supporting stronger standalone PRS signal despite the smaller validation N.

PGS004908 is better supported for the target “kidney cancer” because its endpoint is a direct kidney cancer diagnosis (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: “Kidney cancer”) and it comes from a kidney-cancer–focused multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis identifying susceptibility regions, with a much larger GWAS-hits set (107 variants) and a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.5). PGS000787 is derived from an older 19-variant score (inverse weights) embedded in a pan-cancer risk-factor integration context with an incident-only endpoint and shows a weaker PRS signal (HR=1.15). Both candidates only report full-model discrimination (AUROC ~0.74 vs 0.722) without PGS-only AUC/R2, so metrics are not cleanly comparable; the decision therefore leans on stronger disease-focused evidence and effect-size strength favoring PGS004908.

Both candidates are endpoint-aligned to the target (trait_reported kidney cancer; trait_efo renal cell carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident kidney cancer), use the same covariates, same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same variant count (19), and show essentially identical full-model discrimination and HR (PGS000076 AUROC 0.722, HR 1.16 vs PGS000787 AUROC 0.722, HR 1.15). However, PGS000787 is explicitly a derivative of PGS000076 (“19 variants … with inverse variant weights”), which is a strong negative support signal versus the original, well-defined score. Additionally, PGS000787 reports an R²=0.366 that is not labeled PRS-only and is implausibly high relative to the provided kidney-cancer heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.0178), suggesting non-comparable/full-model or mis-scaled reporting; PGS000076 avoids this suspect metric. With no PGS-only AUC/R² available for either, the original, non-derivative construction (PGS000076) is better-supported.

PGS004908 is better supported for the target trait (kidney cancer) because it matches the broad endpoint directly (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: “Kidney cancer”) and is derived from a kidney-cancer–focused multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis (Nat Genet; BBJ/FinnGen/NCI), whereas PGS000076 comes from a cross-cancer evaluation framework and targets “incident kidney cancer” with an RCC-mapped EFO (renal cell carcinoma) rather than the umbrella label. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2 (both only show full-model AUROC), so performance can’t be cleanly compared; in that setting, PGS004908’s much stronger per-SD effect size evidence (OR 1.5 vs HR 1.16 for PGS000076) and larger, more comprehensive GWAS-hit set (107 vs 19 variants) are the more informative differentiators. Covariate sets are broadly similar epidemiologic adjustments in both, so there’s no clear covariate-leakage advantage for PGS000076 to offset its weaker PRS signal.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target (same trait_reported/trait_efo, same phenotyping_reported familial LOAD, same method and 21 variants, same covariates age/sex, same development cohorts, and both lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2). With metrics missing, the main differentiator is the reported PRS effect size: PGS000054 shows a materially stronger per-SD association (OR=1.73, 95% CI 1.57–1.93) than PGS000053 (OR=1.29, 1.21–1.37), which is stronger evidence of discriminative signal. PGS000053 has a larger EUR validation sample (n=4,792 vs 3,324) and EUR-only evaluation, but validation size is a weak tie-break and does not outweigh the much stronger OR in PGS000054.

Both candidates map to the same EFO endpoint (osteoarthritis, knee), are EUR-only in development/evaluation, and neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (only per-SD ORs), so performance evidence is near-tied (PGS002767 OR=1.35 [1.3–1.4] vs PGS004549 OR=1.3667 without CI). PGS002767 has cleaner, explicitly stated basic covariates (age, sex, PCs, technical), whereas PGS004549 has unknown covariates and is explicitly a risk-factor integration/metaPRS framework (RFDiseasemetaPRS), which raises packaging/leakage uncertainty for a standalone knee OA PRS. Given similar endpoint fidelity and no PRS-only metrics, the cleaner covariate transparency and simpler disease-PRS framing make PGS002767 slightly better-supported on the visible fields.

Both candidates map cleanly to the target concept (trait_reported/trait_efo are knee osteoarthritis), but PGS002767 has better endpoint fidelity in phenotyping_reported ("Knee osteoarthritis") versus PGS002729’s broader "Clinical osteoarthritis". Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS002729’s AUROC=0.66 is a full-model metric with covariates (Age, sex, BMI) and is not comparable as standalone PRS evidence. In the absence of PRS-only metrics, PGS002767’s genome-wide PRS-CS construction with ~1.05M variants plus a moderate per-SD effect size (OR 1.35, 95% CI 1.30–1.40) provides cleaner PRS-specific support than PGS002729’s very sparse 24-variant GWS score with no effect-size evidence. Ancestry is similarly EUR-evaluated for both; validation N is larger for PGS002767 but only a weak tie-break.

PGS002729 is the better-supported knee osteoarthritis PRS on the visible fields because it has clearer endpoint fidelity and more interpretable evaluation evidence: it is explicitly labeled and phenotyped as clinical knee osteoarthritis (trait_reported and phenotyping_reported align cleanly), and it provides an AUROC estimate with CI (0.66, 0.61–0.71) plus disclosed covariates (age, sex, BMI), allowing some assessment of comparability even though it is a full-model metric (no PGS-only AUC/R2). Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Type 1 diabetes) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values (0.921 for PGS000024 vs 0.817 for PGS000023) are not directly comparable as PRS metrics. Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported and trait_efo are identical), but PGS002308 has better endpoint fidelity for a generic T2D target because its phenotyping_reported is general “Type 2 diabetes” whereas PGS001781 is explicitly “Incident type 2 diabetes” (a narrower time-to-event framing). Both candidates are essentially endpoint-identical for the target (trait_efo thyroid carcinoma; trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Thyroid cancer”), same publication family, same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics shown, which are not clean PRS-comparable). Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Type 2 diabetes) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so the full-model AUROC values (0.793 for PGS002308 vs 0.825 for PGS000804) are not comparable PRS metrics—especially since PGS000804 includes BMI as a covariate, which can inflate full-model discrimination relative to PGS002308’s lighter covariates (age/sex/PCs/site). Although PGS001855 has broader multi-ancestry evaluation and larger training/validation Ns, those are weak tie-breakers here versus the stronger effect-size and genome-wide construction signals in PGS004253.

Overall, PGS001536 is far better supported for generic vitiligo risk prediction.
